anomaly_def.Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency limits of the underlying storage stack are saturated, making the device—not the DB engine—the performance bottleneck.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space on data, log, temp, or backup volumes falls to-or below-minimum thresholds, triggering allocation failures or growth stalls.

When both anomalies surface together, the database experiences prolonged and highly variable I/O latencies, escalating wait events, and near-continuous auto-extend or checkpoint activity while simultaneously running out of space. Back-end devices show long queue depths and service-time inflation, while foreground sessions report slow response, "out of space" or "cannot allocate extent" errors, log switch hangs, paused DML, aborted ETL/loads, and backup failures. Space-reclamation tasks, log archiving, and purge jobs slow or halt due to the I/O bottleneck, further accelerating space depletion. Maintenance windows and recovery time objectives are breached as both performance and availability degrade in tandem.

Causally, space exhaustion and throughput saturation reinforce one another: 1) As free space dwindles, the engine issues more frequent auto-extend, file growth, and log switch operations, spiking random and sequential I/O that pushes already-constrained storage beyond its throughput limits. 2) The elevated I/O latency slows background tasks such as log archiving, snapshot merges, purges, and index rebuilds, delaying space release and causing the free-space curve to fall even faster. 3) Checkpoint and flush operations contend with emergency space-management writes on the same saturated devices, risking dead-end stalls where neither throughput nor space can recover without external intervention (adding capacity, throttling workload, or moving data). The intertwined failures therefore create a feedback loop that magnifies both response-time slowdowns and the probability of hard allocation outages.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the number of TCP keepalive messages that can be lost before the server connection to the client is considered dead.
entry.trigger_condition: The number of lost TCP keepalive probes reaches tcp_keepalives_count on systems supporting TCP_KEEPCNT.
entry.workload_impact: The server can consider the client connection dead after the configured keepalive failure threshold.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
